authority: OWNER-RULINGS.md Ruling 25.1 (ASM-0068 opening text ratified verbatim; re-signed against the exact resulting entry)
text:
[[assumption]]
id = "ASM-0068"
description = "`getrandom` over the host CSPRNG returns `Err` or unpredictable bytes."
justification = """
Two units rest their secrecy on bytes drawn from the operating system. The request nonce
`host.request_freshness_inputs` produces is drawn by `SystemNonceSource::fill`, and replay
freshness is worth what that nonce's unpredictability is worth: a nonce an attacker can predict
is a request it can pre-sign a replay slot for. The delegated response-signing key
`proxy.delegated_signing_credential` mints on every rotation is seeded by `getrandom::fill` in
`delegated_wiring.rs`, and a predictable seed is a published private key. Both sites abort on
`Err` rather than continue with the zeroed buffer, and `host.request_freshness_inputs` measures
that every byte of a nonce is written; no measurement can say anything about whether the bytes
that came back were unpredictable. Nothing in this repository can: the property belongs to the
host's entropy source.

So the premise is exactly the split `getrandom` itself draws. An unavailable source is
reported, and every site handles that report; a source that answers with predictable bytes
is not distinguishable from a good one by any test, and that is the case this entry
registers. It is an environment premise and not a cryptographic one: the algorithms consuming
the bytes are `boundary.crypto_primitives`' premises, and this states only what they are fed.

`boundary.os_entropy` names five direct OS-entropy acquisition sites. Of those, three are not
relied upon by any verification unit in this scope: the rotation-backoff jitter in
`signing_plane/mod.rs`, which falls back to no jitter on `Err`; the OCSP request nonce in
`ocsp.rs`, which belongs to no unit; and the audit stream run identity in
`audit_sink/stream.rs`, which refuses startup on `Err` and is used to distinguish process
incarnations rather than as a secret or authorization token. No unit in this scope rests on any
of those three sites.

It stops being acceptable if `getrandom` is configured with a backend other than the host OS
CSPRNG, if a site starts continuing with a buffer it did not fill after an `Err`, or if a host
class is admitted whose CSPRNG can answer before it is seeded.
"""
scope = [
  "unit://host.request_freshness_inputs",
  "unit://proxy.delegated_signing_credential",
  "boundary://boundary.os_entropy",
]
owner = "mats@sundvall.name"
introduced_by = "owner-signature:tcb-os-entropy-premise (r12, fb18b3b14dc7bf01, b243d21bc1720a78)"
review_requirement = "Owner review; any change of `getrandom` backend or version, and any new production acquisition site of OS entropy."
premise_class = "external-boundary"
boundary_owner = """
The HOST OPERATING SYSTEM's CSPRNG, reached through the pinned `getrandom` crate's `fill`: every
call either returns `Err` or fills the whole buffer with bytes unpredictable to every party other
than this process.
"""
affected_contracts = []
tool_specific_mechanism = "foreign-dependency"

text:
[[assumption]]
id = "ASM-0071"
description = "A read of the trust-epoch key over the delegated-signing plane's own connection, issued after an operator's `INCR` on that key was acknowledged, returns a value different from every value that plane read before the `INCR`."
justification = """
The sibling of ASM-0044, for the consumer ASM-0044 excludes by name. `DelegatedEpochWatch` reads
the same shared counter over its own connection and mints under `<base>#<counter>` for whatever
the read returned (THM-0133), and the plane tells the operator at startup that an `INCR` moves
every replica to the next label. That sentence is THM-0133 composed with this premise: the `INCR`
is issued on a connection this replica does not hold, and what a later `GET` on the plane's
connection returns is decided by the store's replication and routing, not by anything here.

Narrow on purpose, exactly as ASM-0044 is: not "Redis is correct", not durability of the counter,
not ordering between replicas, and not that every replica observes the advance at the same time
— only that an acknowledged write becomes visible to a subsequent read on another connection. A
read that returns the OLD value is the case excluded here, and the one that would keep this
replica minting under a label the operator meant to retire. A read that FAILS, or returns a LOWER
value, is outside the premise and handled locally: no label, so nothing is minted.

It is a separate entry rather than a widening of ASM-0044 because the two consumers make
different local decisions with the value — a flush there, a refusal here — and a premise about
what one plane's read means must not be read as an ordering between the two planes'
observations, which nothing in the tree establishes.

It stops being acceptable if the epoch key is served from a read replica that can lag the
primary, if the deployment routes the plane's connection to a different primary than the
operator's, or if the key can be evicted or restored to an older value without that reading as
absence or regression at the reader.
"""
scope = ["unit://proxy.delegated_epoch_label", "boundary://boundary.shared_state_store"]
owner = "mats@sundvall.name"
introduced_by = "owner-signature:asm-delegated-epoch-label-store-premise (r12, 5fc98328eee54d1a)"
review_requirement = "Owner review; any change to the delegated plane's epoch reader, to the label it derives, or to the store topology the deployment documentation admits for the epoch key."
premise_class = "external-boundary"
boundary_owner = """
The shared-state store, across its read-your-acknowledged-writes ordering for the trust-epoch key
as the delegated-signing plane reads it, under the store topology the deployment documentation
admits for that key.
"""
affected_contracts = []
tool_specific_mechanism = "foreign-dependency"

authority: OWNER-RULINGS.md Ruling 29.1 (THM-0049 scope: the X9 sentence of Ruling 28.1 and the 'Three are live' sentence, approved together and applied in one pass; title, statement, security consequence, owner and support unchanged)
text:
[[theorem]]
id = "THM-0049"
title = "Every illegal cross-owner configuration combination is refused at layer A"
statement = """
The cross-machine pass reads classified owner states and validated request selections, never
raw fields a machine already classified, and refuses every relation it declares —
the channel key object living in a backend the deployment does not reach, a revocation deny
list no configured profile will read, and a trust-epoch posture incompatible with delegated
signing. Each refusal is unconditional in the classifier rather than conditional on a caller
having asked.
"""
security_consequence = """
An operator cannot obtain a weaker posture by supplying a combination of individually legal
selections that no machine alone can refuse — a PKCS#11 channel key under a KMS signing
source, silently doing nothing while the operator believes the handshake key is
device-resident.
"""
direct_consequence_severity = "high"
scope = """
Establishes refusal by the classifier over the relations it actually decides. Three are live —
X2a, that a delegated channel key object must name a backend the deployment already reaches,
X6, that a deny list no reachable authorization profile will consult enforces nothing, and
X9 — and those are what a validated deployment is held to.

X9 refuses a `--fleet` deployment whose trust-revocation state has no shared epoch source. It
reads the epoch-source decision from `TrustRevocationState` and the fleet decision from
`topology::classify`; neither decision is re-derived.

It does not establish that the illegal combination is unrepresentable — `DeploymentRequest`
can hold one, which is why the refusal is a check the classifier performs and not a structural
fact. It does not establish that the classifier is consulted on every startup path.
"""
owner = "proxy.cross_machine_legality"
review_requirement = "Owner security-specification review"
supported_by = ["unit://proxy.cross_machine_legality"]
depends_on = []

authority: OWNER-RULINGS.md Ruling 31.1 (82000dd8: the Common-Name identity path is deleted; ASM-0030 'URI SANs, DNS SANs, and subject Common Name' -> 'URI SANs and DNS SANs'; re-reviewed against the resulting certificate identity adapter, which reads only the SAN extension and no subject Common Name)
text:
[[assumption]]
id = "ASM-0030"
description = "The X.509 parser faithfully reports a leaf's URI SANs and DNS SANs, in the order the certificate presents them."
justification = """
`x509_parser` is a foreign ASN.1/X.509 implementation. It is not verified here and proving
it is explicitly not attempted: an ASN.1 decoder is a far larger verification target than
the authority that consumes it, and attempting it would put the slice's proof boundary in
the wrong place.

The assumption is stated as FAITHFUL REPORTING, including ORDER, because order is
semantic in the consuming authority — the first value of the configured field is the
authoritative one, so a parser that reordered SANs would change which identity a peer has
without making any consumer's property false. A parser that dropped, merged, or synthesised
a general name is likewise inside this assumption and outside THM-0024.

It bounds the claim rather than weakening it: THM-0024 is a property of the interpreted
field set, so a wrong parser yields a faithful interpretation of the wrong fields and the
theorem still holds. The consequence of the assumption failing is therefore a wrong
identity, not an unsound proof — which is exactly why it must be recorded rather than
absorbed.

It stops being acceptable if the adapter starts branching on the parser's error kinds
(today it maps every parse failure to one refusal), or if identity interpretation is ever
given a second parser whose field sets must agree.
"""
scope = ["unit://proxy.certificate_identity", "boundary://boundary.x509"]
owner = "mats@sundvall.name"
introduced_by = "ADR-MCPRE-063 Slice 1"
review_requirement = "Owner review; any change to the certificate identity adapter or its parser dependency."
premise_class = "external-boundary"
boundary_owner = """
The pinned `x509_parser` crate, across its ASN.1/X.509 decoding API: it reports a leaf's URI SANs and DNS SANs faithfully and in certificate order, under the default parsing configuration this adapter uses.
"""
affected_contracts = []
tool_specific_mechanism = "foreign-dependency"

text:
[[theorem]]
id = "THM-0041"
title = "An offline-verified receipt proves registration, and its root was never supplied"
statement = """
If `verify_receipt_offline` returns Ok, then: the Signed Statement's own COSE
`Sig_structure` verified under a key resolved for its issuer kid, so the statement is
attributed to the party that actually signed it and to no other; the statement carries the
RFC 9943 §6.1 CWT claims in its PROTECTED header, with `iss` equal to the signing kid, `sub`
equal to the MCP-RE statement subject and the MCP-RE statement content type, so no other
`COSE_Sign1` the same key produces can be read as MCP-RE call evidence; the receipt parsed
as an RFC 9942 §5.2.1 receipt; running the RFC 9162 §2.1.3.2 inclusion algorithm over the
statement's leaf hash at the receipt's leaf index and tree size produced a root that, for an
ATTACHED receipt, equals the root the receipt commits to and, for a DETACHED one, IS the
payload the transparency-service signature was checked against; the transparency service's
signature verified under a key resolved for its kid; where the pinned profile binds the
position, the commitment the service SIGNED equals the one recomputed over that derived
root; and both signatures were attempted only under an algorithm the protected header names
and the resolved key agrees with, out of EdDSA and ES256 and nothing else. No network was
contacted.
"""
security_consequence = """
The root is DERIVED from the statement under verification and never supplied by the caller,
on either payload form. A receipt cannot be made to verify by handing in a convenient root,
and on the detached form a wrong fold produces a different `Sig_structure`, so the signature
simply fails rather than being compared against something the caller chose.

An auditor can therefore check that a record existed without trusting the log to replay
